task.goal: Test whether a classroom plant grows differently under two existing window positions.
hard_constraints: Twelve similar plants, six weeks, no growth chamber or extra lamps.
Do not change watering based on observed growth; log temperature and watering.
Avoid treating one plant as proof; define missing-plant and measurement rules before starting.
task.available_resources: Ruler, daily room thermometer and notebook.
task.expected_result: A controlled small experiment with cautious inference.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Matched-pair randomized comparison at the two windows
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use six matched pairs to estimate whether the two existing window positions produce different six-week height gains. Differences in light and local conditions could change growth; this experiment estimates their combined effect, not light alone.

Before assignment, measure all twelve plants and pair them by starting height and visible condition. Randomly assign one plant from each pair to each window using labeled notebook slips drawn without looking. Keep plants at their assigned window for six weeks. Randomize their order within each window initially, then cycle positions within that window on a fixed weekly schedule to distribute local shading.

This requires similar plants, preferably the same species, comparable existing pots and soil, sufficient space, and an existing way to deliver consistent water quantities. Prespecify the same watering quantity and schedule for every plant, based on ordinary care requirements; never adjust it in response to growth. Record every watering and any deviation. Log room temperature daily at a fixed time and location. A single room thermometer cannot establish simultaneous temperature differences between windows.

The main limitation is that there is only one example of each window position. Results apply to these plants at these windows during these six weeks; they cannot establish a general effect of window orientation.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
Before starting, define height as the vertical distance from the soil surface to the highest living growing point, measured without stretching the plant. Measure weekly at the same time of day, with the same ruler and observer. Record damage, death, and absence separately.

The primary outcome is each plant’s week-six height minus its baseline height. Compare the two gains within each original pair; report all six differences, their mean, and their range against the simple comparator of zero difference.

Prespecify no replacements or invented measurements. A missing baseline or final measurement excludes that pair from the primary paired comparison; retain its available records and report why it is incomplete. Report deaths separately, and call the primary comparison inconclusive if fewer than four complete pairs remain.

The smallest measurement check is to measure every plant twice at baseline, hiding the first readings. If repeat discrepancies are comparable to the eventual window difference, or pair differences have mixed directions, the evidence for a detectable height effect is weak. Height alone does not measure total plant health or biomass.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Weekly randomized window assignments
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Test whether a week at either window changes height growth by repeatedly randomizing exposure. Unlike keeping each plant at one window, this design lets plants experience both positions, reducing the influence of persistent differences between plants. It estimates the average short-term effect of the current window across differing exposure histories; it does not directly estimate six uninterrupted weeks at one window.

Label twelve similar plants. At the start of each of six weeks, independently draw six labels for window A; place the remaining six at window B. Record assignments before moving plants. Randomize spaces within each window and handle every pot equally, including plants staying at their previous window.

Use existing comparable pots and soil, a ruler, thermometer, notebook, and an existing means of giving consistent water quantities. Before starting, fix a common watering quantity and schedule appropriate for the plants. Log all watering and deviations; never adjust watering according to growth. Record room temperature at the same time and location daily. This cannot resolve temperature differences between windows.

The key uncertainty is response timing: plants may respond slowly or retain effects of earlier exposure. Consequently, a small weekly difference would not rule out a sustained window effect.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
Before assignment, define height as soil surface to the highest living growing point without stretching. Measure at baseline and each weekly boundary, before moving plants, using the same observer, ruler, and time of day. Repeat baseline measurements with earlier readings hidden to assess measurement noise.

For each week, subtract starting height from ending height and compare mean gains at A and B. Average the six weekly contrasts, report each contrast and individual trajectories, and use zero difference as the comparator. Repeated observations are not 72 independent plants.

Prespecify no replacements or imputation. A missing endpoint makes that plant-week unavailable; record deaths separately. Declare the comparison inconclusive if fewer than four weeks retain at least four measurable plants per window. Report missingness by assignment because selective loss can bias results.

As a small diagnostic, compare contrasts among plants that switched windows with those that stayed. Opposing patterns suggest carryover or movement effects and weaken a simple current-window interpretation. Differences comparable to ruler repeatability also provide weak evidence.

EXPAND.title: Balanced crossover: each plant experiences both windows
EXPAND.proposal:
Use a randomized two-period crossover to reduce the influence of persistent differences between plants. Each plant spends three weeks at each window, so its growth under one position can be compared with its growth under the other. This estimates growth during successive exposures; it does not directly estimate six uninterrupted weeks at either window.

A teacher owns assignment, care and recording. Label twelve similar plants of the same species in comparable existing pots and soil. Randomly assign six to sequence A–B and six to B–A using notebook slips. At week three, exchange windows without repotting. Set spacing and a fixed within-window position schedule before starting.

Prerequisites are space for six plants per window and an existing way to deliver repeatable water quantities. Prespecify a suitable common watering quantity and schedule, independent of observed growth. Record every watering and deviation, and room temperature daily at a fixed time and place. The thermometer cannot resolve simultaneous window temperatures.

Compared with the prior parallel matched-pair design, the mechanism controls stable plant differences more directly, but adds handling and possible carryover from the first window. Developmental changes or lasting damage may erase that advantage.
EXPAND.experiment:
Before assignment, define height as soil surface to the highest living growing point, without stretching. The teacher measures twice at baseline and weekly thereafter, at the same time; record both readings and use their mean. Record damage and death separately.

For each plant, calculate the three-week height gain at A minus its gain at B. Report individual differences and the equally weighted mean of the two sequence means; balanced sequences help cancel a common period effect. Also report the randomized first-period A-versus-B comparison as a simpler parallel comparator.

Prespecify no replacements or imputation. Require baseline, week-three and week-six measurements; report exclusions and reasons. Stop the crossover interpretation if fewer than four complete plants remain in either sequence. End exposure for a plant requiring rescue care and report that departure separately.

The bounded trial ends at six weeks. Inspect whether sequence-specific estimates disagree, measurements are noisy, or switching causes damage. If the crossover contradicts the first-period comparison or adds substantial damage or missingness, it has not demonstrated an improvement over the simpler design. Inference remains limited to these windows, plants and dates.

EXPAND.title: Improved matched-pair randomized comparison: preserve deaths and missing plants in the result
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: P0’s matched-pair randomized comparison. Preserve its direct six-week comparison, but repair an important weakness: excluding plants that die or disappear could make a harmful window look favorable.

A teacher owns care and the notebook. Before starting, identify twelve similar plants, preferably the same species in comparable pots and soil. Pair them by initial height and condition; use folded notebook slips to assign one of each pair to each window. Keep assignments for six weeks, with a predetermined weekly rotation within each window to distribute local shading. This estimates the combined effect of these two locations, not light alone.

Before assignment, write the watering schedule and delivery method using the existing watering arrangement. Apply that protocol independently of growth; record actual watering and deviations. Record room temperature daily at the same time and place. If comparable care cannot be delivered, postpone assignment and establish a workable common protocol; unequal, undocumented care would undermine the comparison.

Define height as soil surface to the highest living shoot tip, measured without stretching, at baseline and weekly. Define death as no living tissue apparent on two scheduled observations, recording uncertainty. Never replace a lost or dead plant. Report survival out of six at each window, all available individual height changes, and paired height differences only where both endpoints exist. Do not assign dead plants an invented height or silently omit them. Record reasons for missing readings; take a missed reading at the next opportunity with its actual date.

The repair costs some recordkeeping and can leave an inconclusive height comparison, but keeps survival-related losses visible. Conclusions remain limited to these plants, windows and six weeks.
EXPAND.experiment: Before assignment, the teacher rehearses the notebook rules against a simple endpoint-average calculation using hypothetical records containing one death and one missing reading. Check whether the fuller report exposes losses that the average conceals, and count extra recording steps. Simplify duplicate fields if they cause errors, retaining plant identity, survival, dates and missingness. Run one six-week trial; stop exposure for an immediate physical hazard, record any relocation, and treat affected plants as protocol deviations. A survival imbalance or substantial missingness blocks a simple claim that the window with greater surviving-plant growth is better.

EXPAND.title: Masked duplicate measurement to prevent expectation-driven growth differences
EXPAND.proposal:
Use measurement masking as the primary additional mechanism: prevent expectations about the better window from changing how shoots are selected or rulers are read. This addresses an uncovered stage of the experiment while retaining a randomized comparison of six plants per window.

A teacher assigns the twelve similar plants to windows by drawing six A and six B slips. Give each plant a neutral notebook identifier. Prespecify equal spacing, fixed assignments, and ordinary watering times and delivery rules using the existing watering arrangement. Never adjust watering in response to growth. Log every watering and deviation, plus room temperature daily at a fixed time and location.

Before allocation, define the primary outcome as six-week height change, measured from soil surface to the highest living shoot tip without straightening it. Measure weekly at a fixed time relative to scheduled watering. Where a second classroom participant is available, the teacher briefly presents plants in mixed order at a common measuring spot without revealing their window; the reader sees neither allocation nor previous readings. Return plants promptly. This requires safe handling and help, but no additional equipment. If help or safe movement is unavailable, measure in place with previous values covered and acknowledge that allocation masking failed; the randomized experiment can still proceed.

Record survival separately, retain all twelve identities, never replace plants, and leave unavailable height readings missing with reasons. Report individual changes and group averages among plants with endpoints alongside survival and missing counts. Agreement between readers cannot establish a biological effect; masking merely reduces one possible source of bias. Small samples and the single pair of windows limit inference.
EXPAND.experiment: Before allocation, the teacher and helper measure all twelve plants independently, comparing their readings with one ordinary unmasked reading per plant. Record disagreement, total measurement time and handling incidents. Repeat a few readings in mixed order: persistent discrepancies larger than one ruler division trigger clarification of the measurement rule before starting. Abandon transport-based masking after any unsafe handling or if plants cannot be returned reliably; use the in-place fallback. Bound the main trial at six weeks. If masking adds substantial effort without reducing disagreement, it has shown no practical measurement gain over the simpler procedure.
